https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A May 27, 2021 memorandum from Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance & Operations, to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, recommends awarding the District-Wide Fencing Replacement & Installation contract (Public Bid/RFP 9928) to Action Traffic Maintenance, the low qualified bidder among three received. The award covers a base bid plus three years of unit pricing, with a 2021 budget of $150,000 and an estimated three-year project cost of $450,000, funded from the Building Site & Sinking Fund.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A memorandum from the Troy School District Operations Department (1140 Rankin, Troy, MI 48083) recommending a bid award for district-wide fencing work.

Who / when
- From: Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance & Operations
- To: Rick West, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services
- Date: May 27, 2021
- Cc: Donna Havrilla (Business Department); Purchasing Department (File)

Procurement
- RFP / Public Bid 9928: District-Wide Fencing Replacement & Installation
- Scope: remove and replace fencing in poor/broken condition and install new fencing for safety/security
- 3 bids received and opened
- Recommended low qualified bidder: Action Traffic Maintenance (with prior experience in other municipalities and school districts)

Cost / funding
- Base bid plus unit pricing; pricing valid for three years
- 2021 budget: $150,000.00
- Estimated three-year total project cost: $450,000.00
- Funding source: Building Site & Sinking Fund

Purpose
To obtain approval to award the fencing contract to the low qualified bidder so the Operations Department can schedule replacements and installations against the annual budget.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This memorandum, dated May 27, 2021, is from Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance & Operations, to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, on the subject of the Fencing Replacement Bid Recommendation. It originates from the Troy School District Operations Department at 1140 Rankin, Troy, MI 48083 (phone 248.823.4050, fax 248.823.4077), and is copied to Donna Havrilla of the Business Department and to the Purchasing Department file.

The memo reports that a Request for Proposals, issued as Public Bid 9928, sought competitive bids for District-Wide Fencing Replacement & Installation. The scope of work is to remove and replace existing fencing throughout the district identified as being in poor or broken condition and to install new fencing where deemed necessary or requested for safety and security.

Three bids were received and opened, and Action Traffic Maintenance was identified as the low qualified bidder (per an attached bid summary). The memo notes that Action Traffic Maintenance has successfully performed these services in other municipalities and school districts.

The RFP is structured on base bid work together with unit pricing, with a total budget for 2021 of $150,000.00; the submitted pricing is valid for three years. The Operations Department will identify the specific areas needing replacement and/or installation in alignment with the annual budget each year. The total project cost over three years is estimated at $450,000.00. Funding for the purchase will come from the Building Site & Sinking Fund. The memo closes by inviting any questions.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is a design concept and presentation sheet titled Troy School District, Athens High School, Miscellaneous Furnishings, illustrating proposed furniture for an outdoor classroom and interior cafeteria/dining spaces.

The Outdoor Classroom concept is quoted at $52,203.51 (matching the Interior Environments Order 5783 proposal). Its elements include a cantilever corner bench fixed to the wall; a 4-seat carousel provided at both stool height and lounge height with a smooth table top, fixed to concrete; and a custom curved wood bench with a partial back (part of the bench has a back and part does not), fixed to concrete. The layout references existing beds at the back location.

The Cafeteria/Dining Space concept covers two areas. Cafeteria Area 1 is budgeted at $20,000 with a seating capacity of 30. It comprises a booth arrangement of three back-to-back booths with loose chairs on the end (with wheelchair access where the loose chairs are located), using durable fiberglass seats and metal legs and tables with a moisture-resistant edge, plus a high-top arrangement consisting of one 42" high round table with three stools, also with a moisture-resistant edge. Cafeteria Area 2 is likewise budgeted at $20,000 and repeats the same program: a booth arrangement of three back-to-back booths with loose chairs on the end (wheelchair access at the loose chairs, durable fiberglass seat, metal legs, moisture-resistant edge tables) and a high-top arrangement of one 42" high round table with three stools. The sheet is a visual concept accompanying the furnishing proposal and closes with a thank-you.

What it is
An American Cancer Society (cancer.org) informational article, 'Cell Phone Towers,' provided as background for the AT&T cell tower lease under agenda item 9.D at the June 15, 2021 Regular Meeting.

Key points
- Cell towers/base stations receive and transmit signals via radiofrequency (RF) waves, a form of non-ionizing radiation between FM radio waves and microwaves; RF does not directly damage cellular DNA the way ionizing radiation (x-rays, gamma, UV) can
- Base stations are usually 50 to 200 feet high, free-standing or mounted on structures such as trees, water tanks, or tall buildings
- RF energy decreases rapidly with distance; ground-level exposure near typical base stations is hundreds to thousands of times below FCC safe-exposure limits
- Higher exposures are only likely very close to and directly in front of antennas (e.g., on a roof), where access should be limited
- Wood or cement block reduces indoor RF exposure by roughly a factor of 10
- Notes newer 5G 'small cell' base stations

Bottom line
At this time there is no strong evidence RF waves from towers cause noticeable health effects, though this does not prove them absolutely safe; experts agree more research is needed.

Purpose

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An American Cancer Society (cancer.org; 1.800.227.2345) public-information article titled 'Cell Phone Towers,' included as supporting reference material under agenda item 9.D - the AT&T cell tower lease - at the Troy School District Regular Meeting of the Board of Education on June 15, 2021.

The article addresses public concern about whether radiofrequency (RF) waves from cell phone towers (also called base stations) might have health effects. Its central conclusion is that, at this time, there is no strong evidence that exposure to RF waves from cell phone towers causes any noticeable health effects, while cautioning that this does not mean such waves have been proven absolutely safe, and that most expert organizations agree more research is needed, especially on possible long-term effects.

Technical explanation: Cell phone base stations can be free-standing towers or mounted on existing structures such as trees, water tanks, or tall buildings, and are usually 50 to 200 feet high. Cell phones communicate with towers mainly through RF waves - a form of non-ionizing radiation in the electromagnetic spectrum between FM radio waves and microwaves. Because RF is non-ionizing, it does not directly damage the DNA inside cells, unlike ionizing radiation such as x-rays, gamma rays, and ultraviolet (UV) rays that are thought to be able to cause cancer. At very high levels RF waves can heat body tissues, but the levels used by cell phones and towers are much lower.

Exposure specifics: RF waves from tower antennas are directed toward the horizon with some downward scatter; base-station antennas use higher power than other land-mobile antennas but much lower levels than radio and television broadcast stations. Energy decreases rapidly with distance, so ground-level exposure near typical cellular base stations is hundreds to thousands of times less than the safe-exposure limits set by the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) and other regulatory authorities - making it very unlikely a person would exceed those limits merely by being near a tower. Higher exposures may occur on a roof directly in front of antennas, where access should be limited. Indoors, antennas point away from the building and wood or cement block cuts RF exposure by about a factor of 10. The article also references newer, smaller 5G base stations ('small cells') and begins to address whether cell phone towers cause cancer.

It concludes there is very little evidence that living, working, or attending school near a cell phone tower increases cancer risk, citing the low energy of radiofrequency (RF) waves, their long wavelengths, and very low ground-level exposure; the material was developed by AMTA, GSMA, and MMF.

What it is
An American Cancer Society summary titled 'American Cancer Society - Latest on Cell Phone Towers,' provided as background for the AT&T cell tower lease under agenda item 9.D at the June 15, 2021 Regular Meeting.

Do towers cause cancer?
- Very little evidence supports the idea that living, working, or schooling near a tower raises cancer risk
- RF-wave energy is relatively low versus known cancer-causing radiation (gamma, x-rays, UV) and is not enough to break DNA chemical bonds
- RF waves have long wavelengths that can only be concentrated to about an inch or two, making it unlikely they affect individual cells
- Ground-level RF near towers is very low - well below recommended limits and similar to urban background levels from radio/TV broadcast stations
- Most scientists agree cell antennas/towers are unlikely to cause cancer

Other health problems
- High RF levels can warm body tissue, but ground-level energy near a tower is far below the level needed; no published evidence of other health problems

Source
Developed by AMTA, GSMA, and MMF; references the American Cancer Society, a nationwide community-based voluntary health organization.

Purpose
To address health questions tied to the proposed tower.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A concise American Cancer Society summary titled 'American Cancer Society - Latest on Cell Phone Towers,' included as supporting reference material under agenda item 9.D (the AT&T cell tower lease) at the Troy School District Regular Meeting of the Board of Education on June 15, 2021. The document notes the American Cancer Society has updated its public information on cell phone towers and cancer.

Do cellular phone towers cause cancer? The piece states that some people have expressed concern that living, working, or going to school near a cell phone tower might increase the risk of cancer or other health problems, but that at this time there is very little evidence to support this idea. It offers three points arguing against towers being able to cause cancer: (1) the energy level of radiofrequency (RF) waves is relatively low compared with radiation known to increase cancer risk - gamma rays, x-rays, and ultraviolet (UV) light - and is not enough to break chemical bonds in DNA molecules; (2) RF waves have long wavelengths that can only be concentrated to about an inch or two, making it unlikely their energy could affect individual cells; and (3) even if they could, the level of RF present at ground level is very low, well below recommended limits and not significantly different from background RF in urban areas from sources such as radio and television broadcast stations. For these reasons, most scientists agree cell phone antennas or towers are unlikely to cause cancer.

Do towers cause other health problems? High levels of RF waves can cause a warming of body tissues, but the energy levels on the ground near a cell phone tower are far below the levels needed to cause this effect, and there is no evidence in published scientific reports that cell phone towers cause any other health problems. The material describes the American Cancer Society as a nationwide, community-based voluntary health organization dedicated to eliminating cancer as a major health problem, and notes it was developed by AMTA, GSMA, and MMF.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A November 2006 white paper titled 'Radiofrequency and Public Health: The Impact of Radiofrequency Transmissions on Public Health,' authored by David M. Hamby, Ph.D., included as supporting reference material under agenda item 9.D (the AT&T cell tower lease) at the Troy School District Regular Meeting of the Board of Education on June 15, 2021.

Author: Dr. Hamby is identified as Professor of Health Physics (radiation protection) at Oregon State University and a former professor in the University of Michigan's School of Public Health, a graduate of the University of North Carolina's School of Public Health, with 20 years studying environmental and occupational health protection, including six years as a research scientist with Westinghouse. He served on Scientific Committee #64-23 of the National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements (NCRP) and Committee N13.60 of the American National Standards Institute (ANSI), sat on the editorial boards of the Health Physics journal and Environmental Monitoring and Assessment, and served as a technical expert for the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

Content: The paper provides an overview of typical exposure levels and federal exposure guidelines for radiofrequency (RF) electromagnetic waves in the frequency range used by PCS and cellular systems. It explains that biological effects of intense electromagnetic fields are generally thermal and depend on two characteristics, frequency and power, using an analogy to the pitch and loudness of speech, and defines units (the Hertz for frequency; the Watt for power). PCS operates in the 1.9 GHz range, and PCS towers operate at a typical power output of about 200 Watts in each of three sectors.

Exposure limits: RF exposure limits for the general public are set into law by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) based on recommendations from the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), the American National Standards Institute (ANSI), and the NCRP, and are expressed as 'power density' in milliwatts per square centimeter (mW/cm2). On August 1, 1996, the FCC adopted the NCRP recommendation of 1 mW/cm2; Australia and New Zealand adopted identical limits, the Netherlands allows twice that value, and the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) also adopted 1 mW/cm2 at frequencies of 2 GHz and higher. For perspective, the paper compares these limits to human metabolic heat production - about 5 mW/cm2 at rest, rising to as much as 80 mW/cm2 with increased activity.

Key calculation: Assuming a nominal 200 Watts per sector, the maximum power density at 100 feet laterally from the antenna element is calculated to be 0.010 mW/cm2, or 100 times below the NCRP limit - with the caveat that this assumes power emitted equally in all directions within the focused area, whereas the bulk of the transmitted power is normally aimed only at the horizon.

It recounts how the Marshalltown (Iowa) Community School District Board of Education voted to keep in effect a previously approved lease with U.S. Cellular for a tower disguised as a light pole at the high school football field, after RF consultant Marv Wessel of Global RF Solutions presented quantitative radiation measurements rebutting residents' health concerns. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
- Reprint of an AGL Magazine (Above Ground Level) article, May 2009: "RF Measurements Help to Win Lease Approval," about cell-tower site leasing at schools.
- Provided as supporting/background reference for Troy School District's proposed AT&T cell tower lease at Boulan Middle School.

Key story
- The Marshalltown (Iowa) Community School District Board of Education voted January 5 (in the majority) to keep in place a previously approved lease with U.S. Cellular for a tower that would replace and resemble a light pole at Marshalltown High School's football field.
- The vote followed resident concerns about possible health effects of radio-frequency (RF) emissions.

Who/what
- Marv Wessel, Global RF Solutions (Chandler, Arizona), retained by U.S. Cellular to address the board.
- Opponents cited the "BioInitiative Report" (bioinitiative.org); Wessel countered with a Denmark nationwide cohort study (Johansen, Boice, McLaughlin, Olsen) of 420,095 cell-phone users that found no significant cancer link.
- Measurements taken with a Narda SRM-3000 selective radiation meter (spectrum analyzer plus isotropic antenna), covering 50-3000 MHz.

Argument
- Under the Telecommunications Act of 1996, government agencies cannot weigh RF health effects in siting decisions, but landlords may.
- A properly designed cellular/PCS site (antennas 10+ meters up) contributes less RF than the report's proposed precautionary limit of 0.1 microwatts per square centimeter (0.614 V/m); TV and FM broadcast typically exceed it.
- A nearby cell site reduces RF exposure from students' own handsets, held near the head.

Purpose
- To illustrate, by precedent, that RF measurements can address community health concerns and support approving a school-site tower lease.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Reprinted from AGL Magazine (Above Ground Level), May 2009, the article "RF Measurements Help to Win Lease Approval" describes how quantitative radio-frequency (RF) measurements helped persuade a school board to preserve a cell-tower lease. Members of the Marshalltown (Iowa) Community School District Board of Education voted on January 5, in the majority, to keep in effect a previously approved lease agreement with U.S. Cellular for a proposed cell tower that would take the place of, yet resemble, a light pole at the Marshalltown High School football field. The vote came about after residents near the school raised concerns about possible health effects of RF emanations from the tower.

The article notes that although the Telecommunications Act of 1996 bars government agencies from taking into account the health effects of RF when making siting decisions, landlords (such as a school district) may consider such effects when deciding whether to lease. U.S. Cellular retained Marv Wessel of Global RF Solutions (Chandler, Arizona) to speak to board members. Wessel reported that local activists promoted a website opposing the site and that board members and residents referenced the "BioInitiative Report: A Rationale for a Biologically-based Public Exposure Standard for Electromagnetic Fields (ELF and RF)," published at bioinitiative.org. Wessel said the report claims a diverse range of adverse health effects from RF but dismisses a Denmark nationwide cohort study by Christoffer Johansen, John D. Boice Jr., Joseph K. McLaughlin, and Jorgen H. Olsen that included 420,095 cell-phone users and found no significant link between cell-phone use and cancer.

Wessel observed that the BioInitiative Report suggests reducing RF exposure limits without specifying values, other than proposing a "precautionary limit of 0.1 microwatts per square centimeter (0.614 volts per meter)" for outdoor cumulative RF exposure. He argued that any properly designed cellular and PCS site, with antennas at least 10 meters above ground level, already contributes less than that proposed precautionary limit, whereas commercial TV and FM broadcast levels typically exceed it in every major metropolitan location. Wessel presented measurements taken with a Narda SRM-3000 selective radiation meter, a spectrum analyzer with an isotropic antenna calibrated specifically to make RF-compliance safety measurements, capable of discriminating measurements by frequency from 50 to 3000 MHz to isolate each license holder's contribution to the overall RF environment.

Citing the inverse-square law, the article explains that RF intensity from an antenna diminishes rapidly with distance and rarely surpasses the health limit away from the tower, especially for cellular antennas, though workers who come close to FM or TV broadcast antennas may require protection such as an RF suit. Responding to a parent's observation that students have handsets near their heads all the time, Wessel said measurements proved that with a nearby cell site the RF exposure from the handsets would be reduced by thousands of times, concluding that "a nearby site actually helps the issue." The piece was included in the Troy board materials as illustrative background for the district's own AT&T cell-tower lease consideration.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Draft minutes of the International Academy Governance Council meeting of April 14, 2021, held virtually via Zoom and hosted by Bloomfield Hills Schools, with a video recording posted at iatoday.org. The International Academy is a shared International Baccalaureate consortium program, and the Governance Council is composed of the superintendents of its member districts. Pat Watson, Superintendent of Bloomfield Hills Schools, called the meeting to order at 6:01 PM and presided.

Roll call recorded members present as: Birmingham — Dr. George Heitsch, Interim Superintendent; Bloomfield Hills — Pat Watson, Superintendent; Huron Valley — Dr. Paul Salah, Superintendent; Troy — Christine DiPilato attending (non-voting) for Dr. Richard Machesky, Superintendent; and West Bloomfield — Dr. Gerald Hill, Superintendent. Following the Pledge of Allegiance, the council approved the April 14, 2021 agenda on a motion by Dr. Heitsch, supported by Dr. Salah (ayes: Heitsch, DiPilato non-voting, Salah, Watson, Hill), and approved the February 10, 2021 minutes on a motion by Dr. Salah, supported by Dr. Heitsch. There were no requests for public comment on agenda items.

Principal Lynne Gibson delivered a report covering each campus's graduation commencement ceremonies, IB exams, and IB evaluation visits to be scheduled in November/December 2021. At the East Campus she reported math summer school would be hosted for all three campuses and an outdoor classroom added. At the Okma Campus, scheduled summer updates included removing lockers; adding two new bathrooms near the music room; painting all door frames; new theater curtains and flooring in the ISC classroom; 209 new musical instrument lockers; a new rooftop heating/AC unit; replacement of 34 windows; and two new ADA science lab sinks. At the West Campus, summer work included new clocks and PA system building-wide; a new plaza entry to the athletic stadium at Lakeland with a concession building and a restroom building; stadium sound system and power; an improved and expanded student parking lot; and an air handling unit replacement for the competition pool. Dr. Salah thanked staff and students for their resiliency during the year.

Under a Start Time Discussion, Watson introduced the topic of later start times and asked what other districts were doing; West Bloomfield and Troy both reported that later secondary start times had been well received in their communities, while Huron Valley noted considerations around athletics and research and the importance of districts being unified. During public comment on non-agenda items, Joseph Kesto, Filal Erfan, Angela Haddad, Elizabeth Matty and David Day each expressed concern about taking IB exams in person given COVID safety protocols and encouraged administrators to explore the non-exam route, noting a letter prepared by students was being shared with the superintendents. Emilia Askari described efforts to move the Governance Council to an open-meeting forum that provides a platform for student voice and raised continued concerns about transparency. The meeting was adjourned at 6:39 PM and the minutes were respectfully submitted by Pat Watson, Superintendent, Bloomfield Hills Schools.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The June 2021 Principal's Report for the International Academy, the International Baccalaureate consortium magnet program governed by an intergovernmental council of member districts (including Troy). The report reviews the close of the 2020-21 year and outlines 2021-22 priorities across the program's three campuses (East, Okma and West).

Graduation ceremonies, characterized as a success, were held by campus: West on Wednesday, May 26 at the Lakeland High School Fieldhouse at 7:00 pm; Okma on Thursday, June 3 at the BHHS Athletic Field at 7:00 pm; and East on Saturday, June 5 at DTE at 12:30 pm. IB examinations, administered April 29 through May 20 and also called a success, involved 326 full Diploma Program candidates — 94% of the graduating class. Of these, 13 students would have one or more exams graded on the non-exam route due to quarantine or other illness; 18 course candidates were attempting HL (higher level) credit; one student opted to return and take exams in November; and eight students withdrew from all IB exams. An IB evaluation visit was set for Wednesday, November 10 through Friday, November 12.

Return-to-school dates for 2021-22 were listed: Thursday, August 12 for new student orientation, new teacher orientation, and schedule pickup and school photos; Monday, August 16 for staff professional development; Tuesday, August 17 as the first day of school for students; and Friday, August 27 as a no-school day. The report proposes reinstituting a Tri-Campus School Improvement Committee that is both school-wide and campus-specific, charged with preparing for IB evaluation visits, meeting state professional-development requirements, and developing professional development for staff.

The report restates the school's four goal areas. Instruction is to be engaging, innovative, student-centered and inquiry-based, promoting effective and innovative pedagogy. Curriculum is to align fully with International Baccalaureate Middle Years and Diploma Programme standards plus state standards, with a goal of fully implementing and assessing interdisciplinary units (two per year for MYP, one per semester). Culture is to balance the social, emotional and physical health of the community, build capacity for acceptance and inclusion, and foster service learning. Assessment is to fairly evaluate diverse abilities, using formative assessment to build skills and summative assessment to measure mastery, with a goal of defining and aligning the assessment philosophy within departments and school-wide.

A staff survey asked which school goal educators most wanted to engage in for 2021-22; staff at all three campuses chose Culture, citing the need to rebuild community after a year of uncertainty, restore interpersonal relationships and international grounding disrupted by the pandemic, and support students' social-emotional transition back to full in-person school rather than returning to "business as usual." Multiple comments identified assessment as a secondary priority, reflecting a year of more creative, less grade-driven, digital assessment and a desire to analyze which instructional methods from the year worked and to refresh in-person instruction and the Diploma Program.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum on Troy School District Technology Services letterhead (4420 Livernois; phone 248.823.5060), dated July 12, 2021, from Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, concerning a Copier Replacement Lease Agreement.

Soggs reports that the district's aging Konica copier fleet is due for replacement this fiscal year. The affected machines are located at Central Office, the Services Building (Workroom, Teaching & Learning Department, and Special Education), 12 elementary buildings, and the Troy Center for Transition (TCT), with many older machines experiencing regular service calls and downtime.

The recommendation is to replace the Konica black-and-white copiers and color laser printers with Canon equipment as follows: at each of the 12 elementary buildings, one 50-page-per-minute Canon color copier; at TCT, one 40 ppm Canon color copier replacing a Konica B&W copier and color laser printer; in Teaching and Learning, one 60 ppm Canon color copier replacing a Konica B&W copier and Konica color copier; in the Services Workroom / TRC / Special Ed, one 50 ppm Canon color copier replacing a Konica B&W copier, a TRC Konica color copier, and TRC and Special Ed color laser printers; in the Special Education Workroom, one 50 ppm Canon black-and-white copier; and in the Central Office Workroom, one 90 ppm Canon black-and-white copier.

The proposal reduces the fleet by 2 copiers and a minimum of 15 color laser printers and lowers the billable cost per printed page. The current monthly expenditure on the in-place Konica copiers and color laser printers averages just over $6,100 per month in click (copy/print) charges. The 17 proposed copiers carry an estimated monthly cost of just over $7,100 (a $3,112.54 lease payment plus about $4,000 in clicks), an increase of roughly $1,000 per month, offset by removing the color laser printers and two additional copiers. The new copiers would be managed by PaperCut, which should reduce the number of clicks billed to the district each month.

The copiers would be purchased using the MITN Cooperative Bid. The memo recommends a five-year lease agreement with Great America Financial Services at an annual cost not to exceed $37,350.48 for the equipment, plus a five-year per-copy contract with Applied Imaging at set rates not to exceed $0.0032 per impression for Canon monochrome equipment, $0.0049 for black impressions, and $0.059 for color impressions. A cost-per-page comparison shows current Konica black-and-white dropping from $0.00572 to $0.0049 on color machines or $0.0032 on B&W machines, and color LaserJet output falling from $0.0999 to $0.059, for per-page savings of roughly $0.00082 to $0.00252 on B&W and $0.0409 on color. A per-building equipment schedule is attached.

- Tablet-arm lounge chairs

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) 2021-22 Handbook Supplement, distributed to member school administrators. Because of the COVID-19 pandemic and the small number of regulation changes, the 2021-22 MHSAA Handbook (red cover) was not printed; the full Handbook is available to school administrators while logged in at MHSAA.com under School Administrator Services. This supplement contains substantive changes only, to be inserted into the 2020-21 Handbook (royal blue cover); changes are gray-shaded in the online Handbook and explained in red text. MHSAA 2021-22 Membership Resolutions were sent to superintendents via US Mail on May 11, 2021 and were to be returned to the MHSAA by Aug. 1, 2021.

Specific changes noted: Page 25 - the 'MHSAA Handbook Adjustments Due to COVID-19 Pandemic' page is obsolete and to be disregarded, along with references to Page 25 throughout the Handbook. The MHSAA minimum Previous Academic Credit Record (66%) has again been waived for sports played in fall 2021-22; the Pre-Participation physical exam returns for use in 2021-22, while the Health Questionnaire is not in use for 2021-22. Page 29, Reg. I, Sect. 1(E-2) (MHSAA Cooperative Agreements for Multi-School Districts) - the allowance for cooperative agreements in nine sports between public schools of the same district (same governing board) is made a permanent regulation no longer requiring further Representative Council action; the Executive Committee may approve such a program regardless of the combined student enrollment maximum in baseball, bowling, girls competitive cheer, cross country, golf, soccer, girls softball, tennis, and wrestling. There must be a demonstrated history of inadequate numbers of participants; approvals will not be based on financial concerns; the allowance does not apply to public school academies; approval is case-by-case and requires league or conference approval.

Page 31, Reg. I, Sect. 2(A) - Age (only the calendar year is changed): a student who participates in any interscholastic scrimmages or contests must be under nineteen (19) years of age, except that a student whose nineteenth birthday occurs on or after September 1 of a current school year is eligible for the balance of that year; any student born before Sept. 1, 2002 is ineligible for interscholastic scrimmages or contests at an MHSAA member school in an MHSAA tournament sport. Page 33, Reg. I, Sect. 4 - Maximum Enrollment (middle school students enrolled in 9th-grade classes): Int. 24 provides that a student whose classwork is divided between the 8th and 9th grades is considered enrolled in the grade in which the individual takes the major part of the work that term (ties count as 8th grade), and Int. 46 sets the 66% threshold (e.g., 3 of 4, 4 of 5 or 6, 5 of 7, or 6 of 8 high school classes) determining when a student who has completed 7th grade may be considered an 8th-grader, applying only to first-time 8th-graders and not to those repeating the grade. Page 47, Reg. I, Sect. 9 - Transfers (clarification of a full and complete residential change): Int. 77-b allows additional proofs such as proof of rental or completed sale of the former residence and long-term rental/lease or completed purchase of the new residence; the former residence must be vacant of people and possessions or sold/rented to non-family, and may not be occupied for any residential purpose by the student or the student's parents or minor siblings. Page 56, Reg. I, Sect. 12(C) - Limited Team Membership (All-Star): a student who has completed a 12th-grade season in a sport may participate without loss of eligibility for other sports in one high school all-star event in that sport if held after the MHSAA Final, provided the student is eligible under all MHSAA regulations (including academic-eligibility and amateur-status standards), the event receives no financial support from a member school, and participation is approved by the student's principal or athletic director with written notice to the MHSAA.

Minutes of the Michigan High School Athletic Association, Inc. Representative Council meeting held in East Lansing on May 3, 2021, with a cover note directing recipients to copy and share them with their Board of Education and staff; the minutes are published on MHSAA.com, and unless otherwise indicated, changes made by the Representative Council take effect Aug. 1, 2021. Eighteen Council members were present: Eric Albright (Midland), Nicole Carter (Novi), Judy Cox (Auburn), Scott Grimes (Grand Haven), Kyle Guerrant (Lansing), Don Gustafson (St. Ignace), Kris Isom (Adrian), Sean Jacques (Calumet), Karen Leinaar (Bear Lake), Mark Mattson (Maple City), Will McKoy (Romulus), Jason Mensing (Ottawa Lake), Vic Michaels (Detroit), Chris Miller (Gobles), Steve Newkirk (Clare), Chris Riker (Portage), John Thompson (Brighton), and Alex Tiseo (Marquette); Jay Alexander (Detroit) was absent. Administrative reports provided the following data. MHSAA membership during 2020-21 was 747 high schools and 751 junior high/middle schools as of April 1, 2021, compared with 753 and 819 respectively as of April 1, 2019, plus 69 elementary schools with 6th-grade participation. There were 355 high-school cooperative program agreements covering 640 teams (an increase of 16 programs and 33 teams over the previous year) and 86 junior high/middle school agreements covering 330 teams (an increase of 1 program and 5 teams). The most frequent high-school cooperative sports were, in order, ice hockey, boys and girls swimming and diving, girls softball, and boys lacrosse; at the JH/MS level, track and field, cross country, and wrestling. No eligibility-advancement applications were received during 2020-21, the lowest number since the provision began in the 1987-88 school year (comparisons: 3 in 2019-20, 3 in 2018-19, 6 in 2017-18, 5 in 2016-17; the highest was 94 in 1991-92). There were 110 Educational Transfer Forms processed for 2020-21 through April 5, 2021, a figure not directly comparable to prior years because of the pandemic (previous years: 213, 215, 219, 237, and 266); public-to-public school transfers were the most common (67), and the divorce exception (#8) was the most frequent reason (40). Only 6 Travel Forms for Out-of-State Practice were filed during 2020-21, compared with 72 the year before (highest 113 in 2007-08, lowest 40 in 2003-04; the requirement began in 1994-95).

A listing of violations by schools and officials between April 9, 2020 and April 8, 2021 showed totals much lower than prior years due to the cancellation of contests and seasons during the pandemic. Virtual Athletic Director In-Service and Update meetings attracted more than 732 registrants in 2020-21, and two in-service programs for athletic department administrative assistants were planned for September. The MHSAA Coaches Advancement Program (CAP) had already involved more than 2,000 participants in 2021-22, with over 1,200 registrations in CAP 1, and individuals were projected to complete more than 33,000 CAP levels since the start of the 2004-05 school year. The decade-long decline in officials' registrations continued through 2020-21 amid pandemic challenges in recruiting and retaining officials. (The extracted text is truncated at 6000 characters.)

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: An MHSAA informational summary of the Athletes and Officials Accident Medical and Concussion Insurance program, which since 1970-71 has provided excess accident-medical coverage at no cost to eligible athletes (grades 6-12) and registered officials in MHSAA-sanctioned sports. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An MHSAA informational sheet titled 'Athletes and Officials Accident Medical and Concussion Insurance,' expressly noted as not intended to be a complete description of coverage and exclusions, provided to high schools and junior high/middle schools for 2020-21. Since the 1970-71 school year the Michigan High School Athletic Association has provided participants at each member school and all registered officials with insurance intended to help pay excess accident-medical bills for injuries sustained in athletic activities under MHSAA jurisdiction. Coverage is provided for grades 6-12 for all students accidentally injured while engaged in interscholastic athletic activities under MHSAA jurisdiction, namely baseball, basketball (boys and girls), bowling (boys and girls), cross country (boys and girls), football, golf (boys and girls), gymnastics (girls), competitive cheer (girls), ice hockey, lacrosse (boys and girls), soccer (boys and girls), softball (girls), alpine skiing (boys and girls), swimming and diving (boys and girls), tennis (boys and girls), track and field (boys and girls), volleyball (girls), and wrestling.

Eligible student athletes are covered while traveling directly to and from a scheduled event in school-sponsored transportation and while participating in season under the direct supervision of a full-time school employee or designated coach, in sports for which the MHSAA provides a tournament series; the principal must attest in writing that they were eligible under all MHSAA regulations at the time of injury. Students ineligible under MHSAA regulations are not covered, though students ineligible only under local school rules, or those suspended from contests under Regulation V, Section 3 (contest disqualifications), remain covered if allowed to continue practicing with the team. Officials must be on the premises of the contest worked to be covered.

The MHSAA is the policyholder and pays the premium, at no cost to eligible athletes and registered officials. The policy pays up to $1,000,000 in medical expenses after a deductible of $25,000 in paid medical expenses per claim has been met, then pays medical expenses above the $25,000 deductible left unpaid by the parents' or official's insurance or any other sources such as school-purchased insurance. A cash benefit of up to $50,000 is paid if a covered person is paralyzed or in a coma within 180 days after the accident, but not until a physician certifies, after a 16-month waiting period, that the injury is permanent and irreversible, and the payment must result in disability; it is in addition to medical-expense payments. The first medical expense must be incurred within 90 days after the date of the accident, and an accidental death or dismemberment benefit of $10,000 is paid if either event occurs within 365 days of the date. Sideline cheerleaders are covered while traveling directly to and from interscholastic athletic events in school-sponsored transportation and while cheering under the direct supervision of a designated school employee, provided their activity does not exceed the safety norms of MHSAA Girls Competitive Cheer (height of mounts, flips, stunts, etc.). The coverage does NOT cover any out-of-season activities or any activities occurring beyond the mileage limits of Regulation II, Section 6, Interpretation 193, even if not expressly prohibited.

The Claims Administrator is Mr. Bryan Cronen, First Agency, Inc., 5071 West H Avenue, Kalamazoo, MI 49009-8501 (phone 269.381.6630, fax 269.381.3055, bcronen@1stagency.com). The sheet urges boards to ensure all high schools and junior high/middle schools in the district are designated by the Board of Education as MHSAA member schools so athletes at both levels are covered. Separately, since the 2015-16 school year the MHSAA has provided athletic participants at each member junior high/middle school and high school with concussion-care insurance intended to pay accident-medical expense benefits resulting from a suspected concussion sustained while the athlete is participating in an MHSAA in-season covered activity (in-season practice or competition), with a policy limit of $25,000 for each accident.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The MHSAA Membership Resolution form for 2021-22 (for the year August 1, 2021 through July 31, 2022), prepared for adoption by the Troy Board of Education. By the resolution the Board declares that the junior high/middle and senior high schools under its direction are (A) enrolled as members of the Michigan High School Athletic Association, Inc., a nonprofit association, and (B) further enrolled to participate in the approved interschool athletic activities the association sponsors. The Board delegates to the Superintendent or his/her designee(s) the responsibility for the supervision and control of said activities, accepts the Constitution and By-Laws of the association, and adopts as its own the rules, regulations, and interpretations (as minimum standards) published in the current Handbook as the governing code under which the schools conduct their program of interscholastic athletics, agreeing to primary enforcement. Schools that host or participate in the association's meets and tournaments must follow and enforce all tournament policies, procedures, and schedules. The authorization is effective from August 1, 2021 and remains effective until July 31, 2022, during which it may not be revoked.

The completed form fields identify the governing body as the Troy Board of Education, address 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, in the City/Township of Troy, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, with contact e-mail jholmes@troy.k12.mi.us; the record of adoption is marked 'Troy, 20th July' (the 20th day of July, 2021). The MHSAA's address is given as 1661 Ramblewood Drive, East Lansing, MI 48823, (517) 332-5046.

Explanatory text describes the MHSAA as a voluntary, nonprofit corporation comprised of public, private, and parochial junior high/middle and senior high schools whose Boards of Education/Governing Bodies have voluntarily applied for and received membership on behalf of their secondary schools; the association sponsors statewide tournaments and makes eligibility rules for participation. It states that each board wishing to host or participate in such meets and tournaments must join the MHSAA and agree to abide by and enforce its rules, and that it is a condition for participation in any MHSAA postseason tournaments that high schools adhere to at least the minimum standards of Regulation I and the maximum limitations of Regulation II in all MHSAA tournament sports. The junior high/middle and senior high schools to be listed as members and to receive MHSAA mailings during 2021-22 are to be listed on the back of the form. Per the MHSAA Constitution, a school building must have enrollment and onsite attendance of at least 15 students (for grades 6-8 or 9, 7-8 or 9, or 9 or 10 through 12), and a nonpublic school must qualify for federal income-tax exemption as a not-for-profit organization. The resolution must be formally ratified and properly signed; resolutions that are modified in any way or supplemented with letters placing additional conditions on MHSAA membership or tournament participation will be rejected. One signed copy is to be returned to the MHSAA and one retained.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: The 2021-2022 Legislative Priorities adopted by the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA), reviewed by its Government Relations Committee (GRC) on June 2, 2021 and approved by its Board of Directors on June 16, 2021. The platform is organized into topical planks. On School Aid, OCSBA opposes transferring School Aid Fund dollars to balance general-fund deficits; supports additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk, and English Language Learner (ELL) students; seeks to protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax-policy changes; asks that Michigan's Constitution specify the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th-grade public education and opposes any attempts to create private-school vouchers or tax-credit programs; and urges that the annual School Aid Budget be enacted no later than June 1. On Mental Health, it supports increased mental-health services and professionals in schools, with adequate state resources to both educate and keep students and staff safe. Additional planks include Local Control of community-governed public schools with elected boards; Evidence-Based Decision Making through research-based educational legislation to maximize each student's achievement; ending Unfunded Mandates and determining the actual costs of legislation; and the School Finance Research Collaborative (SFRC), urging review and implementation of its recommendations, including additional studies on capital costs, infrastructure, and transportation, while holding higher-funded districts harmless. On Accountability and Transparency, it insists all schools receiving taxpayer funds be held to the same standards as traditional public schools. The Lame Duck plank advocates parameters to address the introduction and accelerated passage of legislation after the November election. Further priorities cover Early Childhood (universal access to high-quality pre-school for four-year-old children), Special Education (full federal funding of IDEA), Broadband Access and Devices (quality internet and proper devices for all students and staff), and Teacher Shortages (state-based programs to address shortages and retain teachers). OCSBA also states support for the MASB, NSBA, and OCSA legislative agendas when aligned with OCSBA priorities. The approval line notes GRC June 2, 2021 and Board of Directors June 16, 2021.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Board of Education presentation titled 'Strategic Planning 2026 Recommendations: Update on Stakeholder Planning,' delivered August 17, 2021, updating the Troy Board on the district's five-year strategic plan redesign. The presentation outline covers an overview of the strategic planning process, the current state, the future state, and a preview of an Accountability Plan. It frames the work as a '(Re)Design Process: See, Engage, Act' and as building system coherence around a five-year strategic plan with a clarified vision and foundation. Guiding questions ask what the district is proud of and challenged by (current state) and what is possible over the next five years (future state).

Feedback from collaborative teams (its 'key wonderings') noted that accountability was missing (data, collective commitments), a desire for clarity and simple understanding of a complex process, better coordination of how the pillars interact, a need to define deep learning, clearer Red Pillar understanding, that Equity and Inclusion were not specifically called out, that the Gold Pillar should include all staff, students, and families, and that the Green Pillar should include a through-line to career with a focus on access and exposure to careers. The presentation cites Michael Fullan's 2021 right drivers for system success (Well-being and Learning, Social Intelligence, Equality Investments, and Systemness) and quotes Louis et al. (2010) on the need for district leaders to be crystal clear and repetitive, arguing that true coherence exists when system members experience it and can 'talk the walk.'

The plan refreshes four color-coded pillars. The Green Pillar ('Investing in Early Childhood to Career') continues investment in high-quality early childhood education, advocates for universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds, and expands college and career pathways and career and technical education, including computer science and work-based learning tied to higher-education and employer partnerships that let students earn a credential and/or college credit. The Red Pillar ('Ensuring a Focus on Equity and Well-Being') calls for safely reopening schools, supporting students disproportionately impacted by the pandemic, funding whole-child supports and community schools with wraparound services (afterschool programs, more counselors, social workers, and school psychologists), and assessing and upgrading facilities. The Blue Pillar ('Deepening Learning for All') builds systems of support that deepen learning and empower student voice, improves technology access and training, and pursues global best practices across content areas. The Gold Pillar ('Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families') focuses on improving educator preparation, strengthening pipelines for underrepresented educators, and providing job-embedded professional learning across the 'OneTroy' community.

Under 'Resource Allocation and Simple Next Steps,' the presentation lists increased social workers/counseling in all buildings; an emphasis on Red Pillar professional learning featuring Dr. Jean Clinton on Tuesday, August 24; 'Media 2.0' positions; sustained support for literacy coaching and literacy interventions; expanded job-embedded coaching for literacy and math; English Language Development (ELD) support; coordinated instructional support; and a delayed-start model providing 90 minutes for collaboration through professional learning. A co-designed Accountability Plan is to be reported out to the Board in the second semester.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: The bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) presented with proposed 2021 amendments shown in red. The document notes prior adoption history: adopted by the Board of Directors on 11/15/2017; adopted by the General Membership on 1/24/2018 and 10/18/2018; with amendments adopted by the General Membership on 9/16/2020. Article I (Offices) locates the association's principal office at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, Oakland County, Michigan, and provides for a continuously maintained registered office and registered agent. Article II (Purpose) states the association's purposes: to advance the quality of public education in Oakland County through the cooperative efforts of locally elected boards of education; to promote high standards in educational programs and services for all students; to make educational-issue information available to board members; to conduct and sponsor meetings and programs in partnership with Oakland Schools; to promote public understanding of the role of school boards and the need for citizen involvement; to enhance cooperation and communication among Oakland County boards; to present a strong force representing school boards' views to political representatives; and to advocate for county, state, and national legislation and governance supporting public education by locally elected boards. Article III (Membership) organizes the association on a membership basis: any publicly elected board of education member of an Oakland County school district, or any elected Oakland ISD board member (collectively 'Member School Districts'), who is also a member in good standing of the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB), is an eligible general member. Each member is entitled to one vote, with exceptions: each Member School District has one vote on selecting a committee chair, on resolutions (Article IX), or on amending the bylaws (Article XVI); such votes are recorded upon receipt of a completed resolution or ballot indicating the district trustees' vote and must be received before the ballot deadline, with results provided to all member districts by the next general membership meeting. Section 3 grants electronic voting to the Board of Directors only, to conduct emergency business, to be reaffirmed at the next board meeting; Section 4 provides that membership is not transferable or assignable. Article IV (Dues) provides the association is financed by an annual MASB grant to its County Area School Boards Association (CASBA) members, by Intermediate School District membership dues in an amount not to exceed the MASB CASBA grant, and by contributions and gifts. Article V (Meeting of Members) requires an annual meeting plus not fewer than three additional regular membership meetings each year to appoint the Board of Directors and transact business, with the annual meeting being the first regular meeting after July 1; special meetings may be called by voice or email by the President or by two or more Board of Directors members with 30 days' notice, and the Board may designate meeting places. The text is an excerpt and cuts off within Article V.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
FY2022 "Equity of Effort" Tuition Calculation for the International Academy – Okma Campus, presented with the Troy Board of Education materials on August 17, 2021. The method sets each participating district's tuition at an equal percentage of its own Foundation Allowance, so that districts contribute proportionally to their state funding. The base tuition rate is $9,200, equal to 108.232% of the reference foundation, and the calculation covers 616 International Academy students drawn from ten Oakland County districts.

District-by-district, showing FY22 Foundation Allowance, IA students, and FY2022 tuition obligation:
- Avondale: foundation $8,529; 24 students; obligation $221,547 (up $747); cost per student $9,231.
- Berkley: foundation $8,500; 25 students; obligation $229,993 (down $7); cost per student $9,200.
- Birmingham: foundation $12,284 (hold-harmless applied at $8,529); 152 students; obligation $1,403,128 (up $4,728); $9,231 per student.
- Bloomfield: foundation $12,364 (hold-harmless applied at $8,529); 140 students; obligation $1,292,355 (up $4,355); $9,231 per student.
- Lake Orion: foundation $8,529; 40 students; obligation $369,244 (up $1,244); $9,231 per student.
- Rochester: foundation $8,529; 113 students; obligation $1,043,115 (up $3,515); $9,231 per student.
- Royal Oak: foundation $9,118 (hold-harmless applied at $8,529); 21 students; obligation $193,853 (up $653); $9,231 per student.
- Waterford: foundation $8,134; 43 students; obligation $378,554 (down $17,046); $8,804 per student.
- West Bloomfield: foundation $9,156 (hold-harmless applied at $8,529); 39 students; obligation $360,013 (up $1,213); $9,231 per student.
- Clawson: foundation $8,529; 19 students; obligation $175,391 (up $591); $9,231 per student.

Totals: 616 students and a $5,667,200 aggregate obligation (billed at $5,667,194, a $6 rounding difference), with a weighted average foundation reference of $8,486.60.

Explanatory notes accompany the table: the initial FY21 tuition rate was set expecting a $600/pupil Foundation proration that did not ultimately occur; FY20 Final State Aid included a $175/pupil proration and $350/pupil of added funding not reflected in the listed foundation allowances; and FY21 carried $65/pupil of added funding based on a 50/50 blend from FY20 to FY21, also excluded from the listed foundations. Districts with high statutory foundations (Birmingham, Bloomfield, Royal Oak, West Bloomfield) have their contributions computed against a capped hold-harmless foundation of $8,529.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Revised budget worksheet for the International Academy – Okma Campus prepared for the International Academy Business Officials Meeting held November 20, 2020, and carried into the Troy Board of Education packet for August 17, 2021. It arrays six columns across each line item: FY20 Final Budget, FY20 Actual, FY21 Proposed (built on a $600 foundation-allowance proration assumption, 108.87% of foundation, roughly $8,597 average per pupil), FY21 Midyear (adjusted to retain within 107.0% of foundation to build reserves), explanatory Notes, and the FY22 Initial Proposal dated November 2020 with a revised factor column.

Revenue: Dues/Fees move from $18,235 actual in FY20 to a proposed $40,000 in FY22, explained as 200 students at $100 club revenue (the club fee had been removed in FY21 due to COVID, budgeted at $20,000 midyear). Interdistrict Tuition rises from $5,045,395 budget / $5,045,947 actual in FY20, to $5,167,044 proposed / $5,602,520 midyear in FY21 (tuition at $9,095, 107% of foundation, 616 students), to $5,667,200 for FY22 (616 students at $9,200, 108.23% of foundation, assuming no increase in the foundation allowance). Shared Costs run $324,117/$353,482 (FY20), $325,000/$314,503 (FY21, revised for a reduced IB Service Coordinator cost), and $320,000 for FY22. Total revenue climbs from $5,387,727 budget / $5,417,664 actual (FY20) to $5,532,044/$5,937,023 (FY21) to $6,027,200 (FY22).

Expenditures with their revised-factor notes: Teaching Salaries $2,379,976 actual (FY20) rising to $2,475,819 in FY22, reflecting a 2.5% increase; Instructional Substitutes held at $100,000 (with a $1/hour graduate-assistant pay bump and added coverage); Clubs and Other Supplementals flat at $75,000; Fringes $489,225 (a 1.25% increase); and Instructional Retirement/FICA $945,812, budgeted at the full MPSERS rate of 28.03% plus FICA of 7.65% because districts receive MPSERS funds directly (no UAAL offset). Contracted Instruction is flat at $54,000 (reflecting an increased Edustaff daily rate and anticipated added FMLA needs); Instructional Mileage $2,500; Printing/Binding $2,500; Equipment Repair/Maintenance $5,000; Equipment Rentals $25,503 (1% increase); Classroom Supplies $30,970 (1% increase); Textbooks $15,000 (history books, with additional teacher input requested); Replacement Equipment $2,500; and Dues/Fees $40,000 (including IB Reath fees).

Counseling costs include Salaries $166,674 (2.5% increase), Fringes $27,801 (1.25% increase), and Retirement/FICA $59,469 at the same 28.03%/7.65% rates, with Workshops ($100), Supplies ($50), and Dues/Fees ($500) held flat. The worksheet, which continues into Health Supplies before truncation, documents the consortium business officials' detailed assumptions underpinning the FY22 tuition rate and budget recommendation for the shared Okma Campus.

What it is
Proposed 2021 resolutions and amendments of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA), a package presented to member districts (including Troy) for review and adoption; most items reference parallel Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) resolution codes. An editing key marks deletions and ADDITIONS.

New and amended priorities

- Broadband Access and Devices: broadband should be included in any federal or state infrastructure plan; supports funding to expand affordable, reliable access and to buy internet-capable devices and software (MASB A-10.30).

Continuing resolutions (adopted 9/14/2019)
- Mental health services and staff training (G 9.01, G 9.05, G 9.50)
- Local control of community-governed public schools (A 10.10, A 10.55, A 12.70)

To set the association's shared advocacy positions before the Michigan Legislature and MDE for the year.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A slate of proposed 2021 resolutions and amendments circulated by the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) for its member districts, which include Troy School District. An editing key marks deletions and ADDITIONS, and most items cross-reference parallel Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) resolution codes.

Three legislative priorities lead the document. The School Finance Research Collaborative (SFRC) item calls for reviewing and implementing SFRC recommendations, including recommended additional studies on capital costs, infrastructure, and transportation, while holding higher-funded districts harmless; the proposed amendment revises a resolution originally adopted September 24, 2019 and is aligned with a 2021 MASB amendment (MASB G 11.01 and A-10.25). Its rationale states continued support for raising all districts to SFRC-recommended funding levels toward equitable funding, and opposition to legislation that would lower any district's current funding. The Broadband Access and Devices priority holds that broadband should be included in any federal or state infrastructure plan and supports funding to expand affordable, reliable access and to purchase internet-capable devices and software (MASB A-10.30), citing pandemic-exposed inequities. The Teacher Shortages priority supports statewide initiatives to address shortages and retain teachers while maintaining quality preparation programs, including incentives to enter and complete teaching programs, incentives to remain in the classroom, and easing Michigan certification for teachers certified in other states (MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority).

Continuing resolutions, described as adopted by OCSBA's member districts on September 14, 2019, include: Mental Health (increased services and professionals, staff identification of mental-health issues, and an MDE model policy; MASB G 9.01, G 9.05, G 9.50); Local Control of community-governed public schools with elected boards (A 10.10, A 10.55, A 12.70); Evidence-Based Decision Making (G 11.01); and Unfunded Mandates, opposing state or federal legislation that increases district costs without full funding (A 10.20). The School Aid section lists five positions: (A) oppose using School Aid Fund dollars for anything other than K-12 education; (B) support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk, and ELL students; (C) protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax-policy changes; (D) constitutionally restrict the School Aid Fund to Pre-K through 12 public education and oppose private-school voucher or tax-credit programs; and (E) enact the annual School Aid budget no later than June 1 so districts can meet the June 30 budget deadline (MASB A 10.25 subparts and A 10.05). An Accountability and Transparency plank supports transparency for all school-aid recipients, including community-governed districts, charter schools, cyber schools, community colleges, and public universities (A 6.65). The extracted text ends mid-sentence on a Lame Duck resolution. As a whole, the document functions as the association's shared advocacy agenda before the Michigan Legislature and Michigan Department of Education.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A three-page summary of proposed 2021 amendments to the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) bylaws, prepared for member-district review, showing current language with additions and deletions plus a rationale for each change. The central proposal adds a new Article VI, Section 1 setting the Board of Directors at an odd number between 7 and 9 (currently 9 for the 29-district, 201-member association), with renumbered sections on board elections, resignation/removal, vacancies, and attendance, and new Article IX committee provisions on quorum, voting, and election of committee chairs.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A summary table of proposed 2021 amendments to the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) bylaws, listing page, article, section, the proposed change (current language shown, added language and deletions marked), and a rationale, for member-district consideration.

Key proposed changes
- Article III, Membership, Section 2 (Voting Rights): retains each Member School District's single vote on committee-chair selection, resolutions (Article IX), and bylaw amendments (Article XVI); committee-chair language moves to Article IX.
- Article VI, new Section 1 (Number of Directors): the Board shall consist of an odd number, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9, with discretion to set the number to meet association needs. Currently 9 Directors serve the 29-district, 201-member association, with no existing process to change that number. Decreases occur by attrition (possibly an eight-member board for up to a year); increases occur by election.
- Section 3 renumbered to 4 (Board Election): by May 1 the Board convenes an Election Committee of the three most recently elected Directors; candidate applications go to member districts; the election occurs at the June meeting; no floor nominations.
- Renumbered sections cover Resignation/Removal (adds an Appendix 1 cause standard), Vacancy (Board may first consider decreasing the number of Directors), and Attendance (three consecutive missed meetings constitute resignation; a Director "may" be granted an excused absence, correcting a 2020 omission).
- Article IX, Committees: adds Sections on Quorum and Voting Rights and on Election of Committee Chairs.

Purpose
To give the OCSBA board flexibility in sizing and filling an increasingly hard-to-staff Board of Directors.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A three-page summary prepared by the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) itemizing proposed 2021 bylaw amendments for its member districts, which include Troy School District. Each row lists the page, article, and section; states the proposed change with current language shown and added language or deletions marked; and gives a rationale.

Article III (Membership), Section 2, Voting Rights: the exception preserving one vote per Member School District on selecting a committee chair, voting on resolutions (Article IX), or amending the bylaws (Article XVI) is retained, with the committee-chair language relocated to Article IX (Election of Committee Chairs).

Article VI (Election of Board of Directors) receives the most substantial changes. A new Section 1 (Number of Directors) provides that the Board shall consist of an odd number of Directors, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9, with discretion to set the number to best meet the Association's needs; the Board is to consider a change whenever an election yields fewer candidates than open seats and before filling a vacancy under Section 6. The Secretary must promptly notify all Members of any change. A decrease is accomplished by attrition, which may produce an eight-member Board for up to one year until the next election, while an increase is accomplished by election under Section 4. The rationale notes the current bylaws neither specify the number of Directors (currently 9 for the 29-district, 201-member Association) nor provide a process to alter it, and that the change adds flexibility given multiple openings and a shortage of candidates.

Subsequent Article VI sections are renumbered. Section 3 becomes Section 4 (Board Election): by May 1 each year the Board convenes an Election Committee of the three most recently elected Directors, who seek candidates giving geographic balance across Oakland County; Board Candidate Application Forms go to all Member School Districts; candidates must apply before the deadline; nominations cannot be made from the floor; and elections occur at the June meeting, by written ballot if candidates exceed vacancies. Section 4 becomes Section 5 (Resignation/Removal): any Director may resign by written notice, and may be removed by the Members or the Board with cause as defined in a new Appendix 1, by affirmative vote of a majority of the Members or Directors then in office (excluding the affected Director). Section 5 becomes Section 6 (Vacancy): upon a vacancy from death, resignation, removal, or otherwise, the Board first considers whether to decrease the number of Directors under Section 1; if it retains the current number, the President notifies Members, application forms are sent, and the Board appoints a member at its next meeting to serve the remainder of the vacated term until the next scheduled election. Section 6 becomes Section 7 (Attendance): failure to attend three consecutive Board meetings constitutes a resignation, though a Director may be granted an excused absence by Board action on a written request to the Board President within thirty days of the missed meeting; the amendment restores the word "may," inadvertently omitted in 2020.

Article IX (Committees) adds new language and renumbers subsequent sections, introducing Section 2 (Quorum and Voting Rights) and provisions on the Election of Committee Chairs. The extracted text is truncated within Article IX.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: The RFP 9929 documentation package for leasing professional office space for the Troy School District’s Oakland County Michigan Works! (OCMW) Troy location, whose lease at 550 Stephenson Hwy, Suite 400 was set to expire October 31, 2021. The One Stop Service Center serves 17,000+ job seekers and hundreds of businesses annually and needed a 3-5 year lease. What it is
- RFP 9929 documentation package (preliminary lease cost estimates, lease rationale, public bid record, lease-cost comparison, and bid scoring) for the Oakland County Michigan Works! (OCMW) Troy office, in the September 7, 2021 Board workshop packet.

Why a new lease
- Current lease at 550 Stephenson Hwy, Suite 400 expires October 31, 2021.
- Facility is the premier One Stop Service Center in Oakland County, serving 17,000+ job seekers and hundreds of area businesses yearly; needs a 3-5 year lease.

Market comparison
- Signature Associates gathered comparable quotes at no cost to the district, ranging from $13.00/sq ft (850 Stephenson Hwy) to $17.95-18.95/sq ft (700 Tower Dr.), all plus electric.
- Estimated moving costs: $150,000-$200,000.

RFP process
- RFP 9929 announced publicly Tuesday, August 3, 2021; posted to troy.k12.mi.us and the State’s SIGMA VSS/DM; sent to five named vendors plus 19 SIGMA contacts.
- Two proposals received by the August 18, 2021 deadline: L. Mason Capitani and Friedman Real Estate.

- L. Mason Capitani outscored Friedman on location/proximity (45 vs 40 of 50) and cost reasonableness (25 vs 20 of 25).
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This RFP documentation package supports the Troy School District’s effort to secure a new lease for its Oakland County Michigan Works! (OCMW) Troy office under RFP 9929, “Professional Office Space Lease.” It was presented at the September 7, 2021 Board of Education workshop and includes preliminary lease cost estimates, a lease rationale, the public bid record, a lease-cost comparison, and bid scoring.

Need for a new lease: The district’s current OCMW Troy lease at 550 Stephenson Hwy, Suite 400 was set to expire October 31, 2021. The facility is described as the premier One Stop Service Center in Oakland County, providing workforce services to more than 17,000 job seekers and hundreds of area businesses annually, and needs a 3-5 year lease to maintain operations.

Cost comparison: Troy Michigan Works!, through director Denise VanHee, utilized Signature Associates (at no cost to the district) to obtain comparable market quotes. The 2021 quotes were: 3221 W. Big Beaver, Troy — $17.00/sq ft; 3270 W. Big Beaver Road, Troy — $15.50/sq ft; 2855 Coolidge Hwy, Troy — $17.50/sq ft; 2800 Livernois Rd, Troy — $17.95/sq ft; 850 Stephenson Hwy, Troy — $13.00/sq ft; and 700 Tower Dr., Troy — $17.95-18.95/sq ft, all plus electric. Estimated moving costs (technology upgrades, server moves, facility build-out, packing, and furniture) were projected at $150,000-$200,000.

Public bid process: RFP 9929 was announced publicly on Tuesday, August 3, 2021 (via newspaper), posted on www.troy.k12.mi.us, and distributed through the State of Michigan SIGMA VSS/DM system (an additional 19 contacts). It was sent directly to five area vendors: Robbins Investments 550 LLC (Rob Krochmal, 248-867-3304); L. Mason Capitani Corfac International (Mason Capitani, 248-637-7795); Winston-Traitel Realty, Inc. (Jeff Raitt, 248-624-7200); Friedman Integrated Real Estate Solutions (Robert Gagniuk, 248-830-9400); and Thomas Duke Realty (Rachel Pannell, 248-476-3700). Two firms, L. Mason Capitani and Friedman Real Estate, submitted proposals by the August 18, 2021 deadline.

Lease costs compared: L. Mason Capitani offered 7,494 sq ft at $104,916.00 (2021-22, $14.00/sq ft) rising to $114,283.50 (2025-26, $15.25/sq ft). Friedman Real Estate offered 7,000-10,000 sq ft at $105,000-$150,000 (2021-22, $15.00/sq ft) rising to $113,680-$162,400 (2025-26, $16.24/sq ft), reflecting a 2% annual increase. All bid amounts are “plus” electric and include daily janitorial services; L. Mason Capitani’s costs include maintenance (CAM), while Friedman’s are additional.

Scoring: On location/proximity to client population (50 points), L. Mason Capitani scored 45 versus Friedman’s 40, credited for close proximity to a bus stop and two expressways (I-696 and I-75) and to the Troy/Clawson/Madison Heights population served; Friedman was near one expressway (I-75) and the Troy/Rochester Hills population. On cost reasonableness (25 points), L. Mason Capitani scored 25 versus Friedman’s 20. The scoring narrative is truncated in the extracted text.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This presentation, “Strategic Planning 2026 – Recommendations: Update on Stakeholder Planning,” was delivered to the Troy Board of Education on September 7, 2021. It previews the district’s accountability plan and describes how strategic priorities will be implemented across the system.

A central theme is distributing leadership. The deck cites “the landmark study of effective district leadership supported by the Wallace Foundation,” which concluded that district leaders must “be crystal clear and repetitive when communicating the district’s agenda for action,” and argues that the best indicator of coherence is when system members experience it and can “talk the walk.” It observes that “most strategic plans are high on aspirations and almost empty on HOW to achieve the goals.”

Next steps for system-level implementation include building cohesive leadership teams (“systemness” across all departments), creating clarity by focusing on a few things, overcommunicating clarity, identifying Objectives and Key Results (OKRs), and establishing timelines. A Cabinet example illustrates “measuring what matters”: an objective to establish clear lines of internal communication and improve central office visibility, with key results such as visiting five classrooms per week, hosting six meetings for all support staff, and issuing Cabinet notes twice per month; and an objective to improve facility enhancement plans, aligning vision with facilities through six collaborative community meetings.

The “Project 2026 Blueprint” organizes work at the district, school, and Troy levels, with teams to report progress to the Board of Education in the second semester while continually monitoring objectives and key results. The Green Pillar — “Early Childhood to Career” — calls for continuing to invest in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for universal pre-school for all three- and four-year-olds, and expanding college and career pathways, high-quality career and technical education, and computer science access, connecting underrepresented students to in-demand, high-growth industry sectors through partnerships with higher education and employers and work-based learning that lets students earn a credential and/or college credit.

An accountability section frames “continuing the world class journey to 2026” as the largest and most important challenge undertaken, and reaffirms the vision “world class for ALL” and the OneTroy values of cultivating a collaborative culture, deepening learning, and focusing direction.

Recommended resource allocations and simple next steps include: increased social workers/counseling in all buildings; Red Pillar professional learning (highlighted by an August 24 session with Dr. Jean Clinton); Media 2.0 positions; sustained support for literacy coaching and literacy interventions; expanded job-embedded coaching for literacy and math; English Language Development (ELD) support; coordinated instructional support; a Delayed Start Model providing 90 minutes for collaborative professional learning; accountability plan co-design with a second-semester report to the Board; summer professional learning dates and new teacher orientation; and an Apple technology refresh in all elementary buildings.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A “Pre-Bond Planning Update” presented to the Troy Board of Education on September 7, 2021, outlining the comprehensive process leading toward a potential bond proposal. It summarizes survey data collection (May-July 2021), a district-wide facilities assessment by Barton Malow, a program assessment by the TMP architectural team, guiding design principles, and a Facilities Review Committee application that had drawn 60 applications. Summary presentations from Barton Malow and TMP were scheduled for an October 5 update to the Board.
